summary.summary: Somerset's year-end treasury report shows borrowing of £716m against a £990m ceiling, with everything compliant — but 39.4% of the debt falls due within twelve months, close to the council's own 50% limit, so a large slice must be refinanced at whatever rates arrive. Housing-account financing costs took 11% of housing income this year and the council's own projections take that to 18.3% by 2030/31. The legacy commercial property portfolio (bought for £301m, written down heavily) is being sold off: £33.3m of sales this year at a £4.7m net gain, £82.3m still to go.

compliance.notes: Strong core treasury strategy: an exemplary Arlingclose-style liability benchmark (charted to 2075 and actively used), thorough counterparty/creditworthiness framework, full indicator suite over six years, and a completed exit review of legacy commercial investments. The weak flank is the commercial/non-treasury disclosure set within the supplied papers - no commercial-income-to-revenue ratio (PI-08), no proportionality demonstration (COM-03) and no service/commercial investment limits (COM-09); much of this should live in the separate Non-Treasury Investment Strategy (Appendix T/E), which was not among the supplied PDFs, and the sterling-only borrowing statement (BOR-03) and specified/non-specified categories (INV-05) are also missing from the TMS itself.

news_drafts.headline: Somerset audit of 2025-26 accounts "in a healthy position", with November sign-off planned
news_drafts.lead:
Somerset Council's audit of its 2025-26 accounts is "in a healthy position", according to its external auditor, the accountancy firm Grant Thornton. A progress report went to the Audit Committee on 28 September. The external audit is an independent check on the council's accounts. Sign-off is planned for November.

The national deadline for completing the audit is 31 January 2027. The council's own report says there remains a risk that it will not meet that date. It scores that risk at 4, calculated as likelihood multiplied by impact, against a target score of 2. Grant Thornton says keeping up momentum in October is important to support the November sign-off.

The report sets out what a missed deadline would mean. It says it could result in "a further modified audit opinion or audit assurance limitations", and could affect the council's future approach to rebuilding audit assurance. The papers describe the consequence as financial and reputational risk. The report uses the word "further", which indicates the council's accounts have previously received a modified opinion. The papers provided do not say for which year.
news_drafts.paper_title: External Audit Progress for the 2025-26 Accounts - September 26 - Cover Report

findings.paper_title: 04z Appendix A - Q1 2026-27 Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: System migration creating backlogs in Council Tax collection (27.44% vs 29.11% target) and Benefits processing; recovery plan targets 31 December 2026
findings.detail: Council Tax collection at 27.44% cumulative vs 29.11% target; Housing Benefit claims processing delayed beyond council's 15-day target due to system migration and final merge of 4 separate Revenues systems in Q1. System downtime June-July 2026 impacted processing further. Recovery plan produced with target return to normal operations by 31 December 2026.
findings.matters: Revenues delays directly impact council cash position. Council Tax under-collection affects the largest single revenue stream. Recovery deadline is December 2026; any slippage would extend collection impact into 2027. Benefits processing delays create hardship for residents and can increase demand for emergency support services.
findings.figures: Council Tax 27.44% (target 29.11%); recovery plan target 31 December 2026
findings.quote: The backlog of work which has been created following system migration has contributed towards this measure not currently being on target... As a result of this merge, system downtime started in June 2026 and finished at the end of July 2026... A recovery plan has also been produced which will monitor actual completed work against forecast completed... The target for this is the end of December 2026.

findings.paper_title: 04z Appendix A - Q1 2026-27 Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Council approving £5.3m two-year investment in SEND services to address assessment backlog and service capacity
findings.detail: In response to SEND pressures, council has approved £5.3m over two years for: restructure and expansion of statutory SEND services, clearing the Education Health and Care Needs Assessments backlog, and expansion of the Preparation for Adulthood function. The rationale identifies 'inadequacy of statutory SEND service structures and capacity' as the underlying issue.
findings.matters: This is a structural response to unmet demand, signalling the council's assessment that current SEND capacity is fundamentally inadequate. Multi-year investment indicates the council expects continued pressure and views this as a design-level problem, not a temporary staffing issue.
findings.quote: Measures that are being taken to address this include a programme of work following approval by Executive of £5.3m over two years. This includes: restructure and expansion of statutory SEND services; clearing the backlog of EHCNAs (Education, Health and Care Needs Assessments); and expansion of the Preparation for Adulthood function within the Virtual School

findings.paper_title: 04z Appendix A - Q1 2026-27 Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Care Act assessments at 53.2% completed on time (target 75%); SEND assessments at 46.4% within 20-week statutory window
findings.detail: Care Act statutory assessments: 53.2% on time against 75% target, impacted by 'demand levels, workforce capacity challenges and existing waiting lists'. SEND Education Health and Care Plan Assessments: 46.4% completed within the 20-week statutory window. Council notes 'Education Health and Care Plan Assessments continue to take longer than the 20- week target.' Both are part of the overspent Children's and Adult Services budgets.
findings.matters: These are statutory obligations with legal consequences for delay. Dual failures in both adult and children's social care assessment timeliness suggest structural under-resourcing across social care, not isolated service issues.
findings.figures: Care Act: 53.2% on time (target 75%); SEND: 46.4% within 20 weeks
findings.quote: Current performance is 53.2%, a slight reduction from 55.3% reported at the end of Q4 2025/26, and remains below target. Demand levels, workforce capacity challenges and existing waiting lists continue to impact timeliness.

findings.paper_title: 04z Appendix A - Q1 2026-27 Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Learning Disabilities pooled budget identified as primary cause of £11.839m Adult Services overspend
findings.detail: The £11.839m Adult Services and Housing overspend is attributed to 'the Learning Disabilities pooled budget'. No further detail provided on drivers (demand, unit cost inflation, partner contribution shortfall). Pooled budgets involve partner funding (likely health/CCG); overspend may indicate either partner shortfall or unmet demand exceeding all partners' contributions.
findings.matters: Learning Disabilities is a high-cost area. As a pooled budget, the council cannot unilaterally control costs or demand; partner funding failures directly impact the council's position. This is the second-largest component of the total overspend.
findings.quote: Adult Services and Housing (£11.839m), largely due to the Learning Disabilities pooled budget

findings.paper_title: 04z Appendix A - Q1 2026-27 Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Children in residential care at 59% vs 10.3% target; 14.2% experiencing 3+ placements; £14.636m overspend
findings.detail: 59% of children in care are in residential settings (target 10.3%), indicating insufficient local fostering and in-house provision. 14.2% of children have 3+ placements in the year (target 10%). Council assessment: 'This is a sufficiency issue and work is underway to improve sufficiency in local homes in Somerset.' This is the largest component of the Q1 overspend, as residential and out-of-county placements cost significantly more than local in-house provision.
findings.matters: This is a structural insufficiency, not a temporary budget variance. Unless local sufficiency is improved, the council will face recurring overspends in this costly area. Out-of-county placements also increase safeguarding and supervision complexity.
findings.figures: 59% in residential care (target 10.3%); 14.2% with 3+ placements (target 10%); £14.636m overspend
findings.quote: The main pressures are within Children, Families and Education Services (£14.636m), driven by higher than budgeted residential placements and unregistered placement costs
